id-eq-const.note: The primary key as a filterable attribute (#376). Chroma's `where` filters METADATA only — the document id is addressed by the separate `ids` argument — so this works only because the harness mirrors the id into a metadata key and the mapper points `request.resource.id` at it. Its five id-* siblings compare the key against a second key or a computed operand and are fail-closed.

in-empty.note: The plan kind, not a filter: `x in []` is false for every document, so the planner folds it to ALWAYS_DENIED and the caller short-circuits without querying Chroma at all. There is no `filters` key to emit.

in-single.note: The planner folds a single-element `in` to an equality before the adapter ever sees it, so this is `$eq` rather than a one-element `$in`. Pinned because it is a shape a reader would otherwise expect to be `$in` and reach for the wrong assertion.

not-and.note: De Morgan, because Chroma's `Where` grammar has no `$not` and no `$nor`. `!(aBool && aString != 'one')` has to arrive as `$or` of the two inverted leaves; a `$not` left in the tree would be rejected by Chroma at query time rather than by the adapter at translation time.

p-has.note: The corpus's one known planner divergence for this adapter. `has()` over a missing attribute folds to ALWAYS_ALLOWED, and the adapter faithfully emits the empty filter that plan kind means — which selects every document, while `check()` denies the ones missing the attribute. Pinned here because the over-grant is the PLANNER's, not the translation's: an adapter that quietly narrowed it would be inventing a filter the plan does not carry. See the README's `Conformance contract`.

p-in-null-multi.note: `$in` over an OPTIONAL metadata key, which is sound where `$nin` is not: a document missing `aOptionalString` fails `$in` the way CEL's missing-attribute error denies it, while `$nin` would match it and over-grant. The asymmetry is the whole reason `required` gates only the negative operators.

pv-exists-unrolled.note: Below the planner's 10-element unroll cap, `P.attr.fewTeams.exists(t, R.attr.aOptionalString == t)` arrives as a plain nested `or` chain and translates. Above it — `pv-exists`, over the eleven-element `manyTeams` — the macro ships as a lambda over a literal value list and throws. That data-dependent cliff is why the README tells integrators to spell membership as `R.attr.x in P.attr.xs`, which is one `$in` at every size.

rel-eq-hop.note: The corpus's one real to-one relation (#375), flattened onto a dotted metadata key. Chroma has no join, so the chain resolves only because the application stored `parent.aString` on the document itself — and every `parent.*` mapping stays optional, because 8 of the 21 seeds have no parent, which is why the NEGATED hop shapes are fail-closed.

vf-le.note: Value-first. The plan reads `3 <= R.attr.aNumber`, and the emitted operator is the MIRRORED one — `$gte` against the metadata key, not `$lte`. Emitting the operator as written is the operand-inversion bug the shared corpus exists to catch, and it is invisible to a harness whose seeds happen to be symmetric around the threshold.

vf-ne.note: The only inequality shape in this asset that is safe, and it is safe only because the corpus mapper declares `aString` as `required: true`. Chroma's `$ne` MATCHES a document missing the key, where CEL raises a missing-attribute error and the PDP denies — so without that declaration this action throws. The "clearing required moves exactly the actions that emit an inequality" assertion is what keeps the two in step.
